subject: arcadeCabinet
pitch:
Category: Object.
Subject: 1980s arcade cabinet.
Style: synthwave.
reasoning:
I'm planning a synthwave arcade cabinet model at realistic scale, roughly 1.8m tall, with a dark navy body, neon magenta/cyan accents, a sun marquee, and a grid screen, built from box primitives with extrusion and glow effects.

I'm sketching the cabinet's side profile as a polygon in z-y coordinates—base, angled control panel, recessed monitor bezel, and marquee top—then extruding it along x to form the two symmetric side panels.

For the paint, I'm designing a procedural shader for the side art: dark navy-to-purple gradient with diagonal magenta/cyan neon stripes based on surface coordinates, plus stars.

Now I'm laying out the body geometry: the front lower panel with the coin door area, back panel, top, and a tilted control panel box angled from the front lip up to the deck surface, with specific box dimensions for width and depth.

I'm working out the rotation angle for the control panel so it tilts slightly upward toward the back, calculating about a 10-degree tilt about the X axis to match the rise-over-run of the panel height difference. Next I plan a textured front board below the panel to depict the coin door using a plane geometry decal.

I'm placing the front decal plane at the correct z-offset to sit flush against the front face box, confirming static parts without joints are fine here. Then I'm figuring out the slant angle for the monitor bezel, computing roughly 7.8 degrees from vertical based on the bezel's rise and run, before building that angled box part.

I'm working out which direction to rotate the monitor screen so its normal faces the viewer correctly, since the bezel leans forward at the top and I need the screen's surface and texture to tilt to match that angle rather than point the wrong way.

Now I'm setting up the frame and screen geometry, positioning the inner screen plane slightly offset from the bezel along the surface normal, and planning the SVG texture to look like a synthwave sun over a grid with a retro arcade game scene.

Then I'm designing the marquee: a glowing neon sign plane positioned above, with "STAR RUNNER" text and cyan/magenta trim strips around it for that arcade cabinet glow, plus edge-lighting strips along the cabinet's side profile.

Switching to capsules for smoother outline corners, then moving to the control panel details: joystick, colored buttons with glow, and a decal plane on the deck tilted to match the cabinet's angled top with graphics like "PLAYER 1" text.

Working through the tilt math, I'm confirming the deck normal rotates forward as the surface rises toward the back, so the plane's orientation needs its "up" direction pointing toward the back so any text reads upright from the player's viewpoint.

Now I'm setting up a local coordinate helper for placing joysticks and buttons on the deck surface, computing positions relative to the deck center using the tilted axes and the surface thickness, then starting to lay out the left joystick position with a red ball marker before placing the buttons.

Next I'm designing the coin door graphic with glowing red/yellow slots, return buttons, and a "25¢" label, then planning the front lower panel artwork as a synthwave-style gradient with magenta/cyan stripes and "INSERT COIN" text.

I'm also positioning the control panel's front lip as an angled box tilted forward, adding a kick plate with a glowing cyan floor strip beneath it, and planning extruded side panel artwork featuring a large sun graphic and stripe patterns using surface coordinates.

Writing side paint shader...

Still working out panel geometry...

I also need to close a top horizontal box near y1.81, then handle the small visible gap between the bezel top and marquee bottom by adding an angled filler box and a dark "speaker grille" box tucked under the marquee. I'm also checking whether the cavity between the control deck and bezel base needs its own closing piece.

Beyond that, I'm skipping unnecessary details like T-molding, coin returns, and leg levelers since they're either covered by texture or not meaningfully visible, and instead focusing on the marquee's neon glow bar and its texture — a dark gradient background with a sunburst behind bold italic "STAR RUNNER" text styled with cyan stroke and magenta shadow plus scattered small stars.

Now I'm designing the screen texture: a dark purple-to-magenta horizon with a sun, cyan mountain outlines, a retro perspective grid below the horizon, score text in cyan and magenta, pixel-art aliens, a ship, and a bullet, with a vignette overlay for CRT darkening at the corners. I'm also sketching the control panel texture with neon outlines around the joystick zone, "PLAYER 1" and "START" text, arrows, and magenta grid lines, sized to fit the deck's top surface placement just above the cabinet center.

I'm figuring out the glow wrapper logic -- cloning materials with emissive properties for the marquee, screen, neon rods, slot parts, and buttons, making sure textured parts still render their own colors through the map while glowing. I'm also planning a custom gradient-based paint function with subtle noise for the side body panels, reused for front and back, and sketching the front panel texture with a navy-to-purple gradient, a metallic coin door with two slots, a coin return, and "INSERT COIN 25¢" text along with a decorative star element.

Now I'm computing the geometry for the control deck's angled surface, deriving its normal and tangent vectors from a 10-degree tilt to position deck points correctly in 3D space, and checking that the deck slopes upward toward the back consistent with the cabinet's side profile.

Then I'm shifting the deck center down slightly so the box's top surface aligns with the profile line instead of poking above it, and moving on to constructing the joystick and buttons—placing a cylindrical stick with a red ball tip, a black base disc, and several button cylinders at specific offsets along the deck's tilted surface.

Simplifying to just one start button near the back edge to avoid collisions with the fire buttons, keeping it clear of the deck boundary.

For the rod structures I'll use capsule geometry between two points, which returns a sweep mesh compatible with the glow effect. For the neon profile outline, I'll alternate colors between consecutive edge pairs—cyan for front edges, magenta for back edges, keyed off index parity. I'm also considering adding thin cyan frame boxes around the bezel to give the inner screen glow more definition.

Now I'm adding glow rods around the marquee instead of the screen, forming a cyan rectangle frame at a fixed z-depth using the marquee's corner coordinates. I'm skipping a floor grid glow effect, then moving on to defining the alien sprite pixel patterns as rows of characters representing an invader shape, which I'll turn into SVG rects at a small scale.

Writing invader path logic...

Then I'm sketching the horizon grid lines radiating from a vanishing point down to the bottom edge, with horizontal lines spaced using a quadratic curve for perspective, all in cyan, plus a retro sun with horizontal strips masking its lower half to create the classic striped-sun look.

Setting up the sky gradient from deep purple at the top through magenta near the horizon to dark purple below it, keeping the palette compact, then starting on a generic body paint function that mixes colors based on vertical position with some noise added for texture.

Now I'm defining helper functions for building geometry — a box helper for creating colored, positioned boxes, extruding outlines for the arcade cabinet sides with proper thickness and normals, and working out the screen bezel's position within the cabinet.

Checking the marquee box placement — making it a solid box covering top and sides so I don't need a separate top slab, positioning it so the front face lines up near the plane boundary.

Working out the front panel box dimensions and placement, plus the texture plane for the cabinet face, and adding glow strips near the floor for ambient lighting accents.

Now computing the lip box dimensions using the hypotenuse of the two offsets, and setting its rotation angle to tilt it correctly.

Picking a deep magenta flat color for the lip, with a thin cyan strip accent, then writing it all out.
